questions.q: What specific noise problem limited the earlier charge qubit design?
options: Charge noise -- tiny, uncontrolled fluctuations in stray electric charge that directly shift the qubit's energy levels because its behavior depends sharply on the exact number of Cooper pairs on a small island
Thermal noise from the dilution refrigerator warming up unexpectedly
Magnetic field noise from nearby power lines
Acoustic vibration noise from the building
questions.explain: The charge qubit's energy levels depend sharply on the precise charge state of a small superconducting island, so small, uncontrolled charge fluctuations in the environment directly degrade its coherence and control.

questions.q: How does the transmon design reduce sensitivity to charge noise compared to a plain charge qubit?
options: By adding a large shunting capacitor in parallel with the Josephson junction, which spreads the quantum state across many charge configurations and flattens the energy levels' sensitivity to exact charge
By removing the Josephson junction entirely
By operating at a much higher temperature than other superconducting qubits
By using a magnetic field to cancel out charge fluctuations
questions.explain: The large shunting capacitor is the defining feature of the transmon -- it washes out the sharp charge-dependence that made the original charge qubit so vulnerable to charge noise.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff the transmon design accepts in exchange for reduced charge-noise sensitivity?
options: Reduced anharmonicity -- the gap between the 0->1 and 1->2 transition frequencies becomes smaller, leaving less room to design clean control pulses
A complete loss of the ability to be read out with microwave pulses
A requirement to operate at room temperature instead of millikelvin temperatures
An increase in electrical resistance in the circuit
questions.explain: The same large capacitance that suppresses charge noise also shrinks the circuit's anharmonicity, which is a real design tradeoff between noise immunity and control-pulse separation.

questions.q: Roughly what order of magnitude is a typical transmon's anharmonicity, compared to its main transition frequency (typically a few GHz)?
options: On the order of a few hundred megahertz, roughly -- noticeably smaller than the main transition frequency
Exactly identical to the main transition frequency
On the order of a few hertz
Larger than the main transition frequency by a factor of ten
questions.explain: Transmon anharmonicity is typically a few hundred MHz, roughly, which is meaningfully smaller than the several-GHz main transition frequency -- small enough to require careful pulse shaping but large enough to still be usable.

questions.q: Which major superconducting quantum computing efforts build their processors around transmon-family qubits?
options: IBM, Google, and Rigetti all build around transmon-family qubits, despite differing in fabrication details, connectivity, and control electronics
Only IBM uses transmons; Google and Rigetti use an entirely different qubit type
None of them use transmons -- they all use trapped-ion qubits
Only academic research labs use transmons; commercial companies use a different design
questions.explain: Despite real differences in how each company fabricates and wires its chips, IBM, Google, and Rigetti all build on transmon-variant qubits -- it's the common foundation across the major superconducting efforts.
